summary: This memo states the requirements for establishing a new Domain and introduces the limited set of top-level domains. It is an official policy statement of the IAB and DARPA.

eli5.summary: This note lists the rules for creating a new part of the naming system and names the first few big groups, like the top shelves of a filing cabinet.

subtitle: The 1984 policy that said who may create a domain, and named the first handful of top level domains.

tldr.problem: The new tree-structured domain naming system needed rules for who may create a domain, and a small first set of top level names to hang everything from.
tldr.mechanism: Domains are administrative entities. Each needs a responsible person, a robust domain server, a minimum size and registration with the level above. The memo sets the initial top level domains: ARPA, GOV, EDU, COM, MIL, ORG, country codes and multiorganizations.
tldr.outcome: It is an official policy statement of the IAB and DARPA from October 1984. It plans for the temporary ARPA top level domain to go away and describes hosts moving into other domains.

today: RFC 920 is a 1984 policy statement of the IAB and DARPA, and its status is listed as Unknown here. The text covers only the plans of October 1984, including the planned end of the ARPA top level domain, and says nothing about later events. It restates RFC 881, and the domain server concepts are in RFC 882 and RFC 883.

sections.title: Purpose of Domains
sections.content:
RFC 920 is a policy statement on the requirements for establishing a new domain in the ARPA-Internet and the DARPA research community. It restates and refines the requirements first described in RFC 881, adds considerable detail, and introduces the limited set of top level domains.

Domains are administrative entities. Their purpose is to divide the name management required of a central administration and assign it to sub-administrations. There are no geographical, topological or technological constraints on a domain, and the hosts in one need not share hardware, software or even protocols. Most of the requirements exist to ensure responsible administration.

The domain system is a tree-structured global name space with a few top level domains, subdivided into second level domains, then third level domains, and so on.
sections.eli5: Domains are like neighborhoods. Each one has someone in charge of names, so no single office has to handle every name in the world.

sections.title: The Initial Top Level Domains
sections.content:
The initial top level names fall into groups. ARPA is temporary and covers the current ARPA-Internet hosts. The categories are GOV (government), EDU (education), COM (commercial), MIL (military) and ORG (any other domains meeting the second level requirements). Countries use the two-letter code from the ISO standard for country names. A large, international multiorganization that cannot easily be classified may also be a top level domain.

The motivation for general categories is to provide an organization name free of undesirable semantics. Each top level domain has an administrator and an agent. DARPA administers all of the initial ones except MIL, which is administered by DDN-PMO, and the Network Information Center (NIC) is the agent for all of them. No country or multiorganization domains had yet been established.

The memo gives illustrative examples that it calls fictions of the authors' creation, such as hosts under UC.EDU and MIT.EDU, and a consortium called CSNET that might qualify as a top level domain under the multiorganization rule.
sections.eli5: The biggest shelves in the cabinet are named for broad groups, like schools, companies, governments and countries.

sections.title: General Requirements on a Domain
sections.content:
To establish a domain it must be responsibly managed. The memo lists these requirements:

  • Responsible person: someone with authority over names in the domain and technical expertise, who is available to receive reports of problems and see that they are fixed.
  • Domain servers: a robust, reliable service. One way to meet this is at least two independent domain servers, as physically independent as possible with no common point of failure. A domain may cooperate with another domain, or arrange for a third party to run service.
  • Minimum size: top level domains must be specially authorized and in general only for domains expected to have over 500 hosts. For a second level domain the guideline is over 50 hosts, a very soft requirement.
  • Registration: the administrator of a level N domain registers with the registrar of the level N-1 domain, which must be satisfied that the requirements are met.

Third through Nth level domains must meet whatever the administrator of the next higher level sets, which may be more or less strict. Minimum size requirements would be expected to decrease at each level.
sections.eli5: To open a new drawer you need a grown-up in charge, a backup copy of your list in case one gets lost, and permission from the drawer above you.

sections.title: Registration Questions and the NIC
sections.content:
The NIC is the registrar of all top level domains and the administrator of several of them, including registering the second level domains within them. The memo hopes that other authorities will later take over some of these domains and does not want the NIC to administer all top level domains forever.

To establish a domain, eight kinds of information go to the NIC Domain Registrar: the top level domain to join, the administrative head, the domain technical contact, the zone technical contact, the domain name (up to 12 characters), a description of the servers and the date they will be operational, a description of the server machines, and estimated host counts initially and at one, two and five years. The memo gives examples for each.
sections.eli5: Opening a drawer means filling out a form: who is in charge, who to call when something breaks, and how many things you expect to store.

sections.title: The ARPA Domain and Impact on Hosts
sections.content:
The ARPA domain was selected at first because DARPA hosts were thought to make up a domain, but the memo sees no strong motivation for a top level ARPA domain. The plan is for it to go out of business as soon as possible. Existing hosts should consider their options for a few months, then join another domain. There will probably be a second level domain ARPA.ORG for experimental purposes.

DDN hosts that do not take part will keep using the HOSTS.TXT file maintained by the NIC, and will change names from host.ARPA to, for example, host.DDN.MIL on a schedule set by the DDN-PMO.

The domain is part of the host name, so changing domains changes the name. Old references in host tables, mailing lists, message headers and printed directories go out of date. Experience suggests renaming a host is somewhat painful, so the memo recommends careful thought about the place in the hierarchy. The owner of a host and a domain administrator must reach an understanding about the host being in the domain.
sections.eli5: If you move to a different drawer your label changes, and everyone who knew your old label has to learn the new one. So choose your spot with care.
